en: Semetey was born greater.
If you have heard reports about yourself,
And keep believing your wife,
Here is the city of Baashaluu,
And here am I—cut off my head!"
Unerring Azhybay
Had spoken his fitting words;
He revealed his eloquence.
Azhybay, eloquent beyond others,
Every weighty word
Of prince Semetey—
He drove it into his heart.
Then Semetey,
Hearing many kinds of words from Azhybay,
Found all he said persuasive;
Thinking, "She is acting like a woman,"
He came to hate Aychürök.
For maligning her own elder brother,
God has struck her!
His eyes reddened like a lion's;
The fearsome leopard
Showed his venomous face
And now stared at Chürök.
Unable to bear his anger,
What could dear Chürök do?
She hurried forward at an amble;
Unable to bear his venom,
While the gray-maned lion stared,
She cowered behind the curtain.
Azhybay, son of Azhy,
And Tümönbay, son of Tülkü,
Now put the day in writing
And received the reckoning of the date.
When seven days had passed,
Brave Toltoy as bridegroom—
Let him come to Aychürök.
Azhybay, son of Azhy,
Now made the pledge.
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Was twelve years old then;
He was a remarkable one,
A glowing red ember,
With no one like him in the world,
A prodigy born among men,
With no one like him among mortals.
The horse he rode was gray;
From heroic Sultan Alma—
Külchoro, left as a gift
Whose father was a lion lord,
Was a man a spear's height tall.
In the palace with iron doors,
In Aychürök's splendidly built
Fortress,
When the pledged day was fulfilled,
When the time came
For Toltoy the bridegroom to arrive,
The vast Afghan host was there,
The common people and their khan;
Khan Akun was there too,
Azhybay, son of Azhy,
Tümönbay, son of Tülkü,
And all those who gave wise counsel—
Every wise man was there.
"Khan Semetey, our son-in-law, has arrived,"
They said;
The many Afghans in the city
Had heard the news,
As had their impetuous Bek Akun.
Saying, "Lion Semetey the bridegroom
Will rescue her
From Toltoy of the Zhediger,
And raise a great tumult,"
All the Afghans gathered
And invoked Bahauddin.
If the prose tale were told on,
The tale of Choro, son of Almambet,
Would never be exhausted.
At twelve years old, that remarkable boy
Asked leave of Semetey,
And bowed as he said:
"Blood-taking elder brother, leopard,
My saint who made me your dependent,
Give me your horse no bullet can catch;
Give me your coat no bullet can pierce.
If you give me both, I shall put them on
And learn what tyranny
Arrogant Toltoy possesses!
If God's written decree
Is inscribed upon my brow, I shall see it;
I shall die while jousting
Against Toltoy of the Zhediger!
That hulking infidel Toltoy,
The hero coming as bridegroom—
Whichever of Kozho and Toltoy
Falls into my hands,
If my death has come, I shall die;
If it lies within my power,
I shall make a spectacle of them for you!
I intend to break their ranks
In a clash of spears and see;
If death comes to me from God,
I intend to die!
Whichever of Toltoy and Kozho
Falls into my hands,
I intend to make him a spectacle
And present him to you.
That consummate prince Toltoy,
That would-be brother-in-law—
Let us be drenched in bloody blood,
Let us stand and fight without fleeing,
Let us grapple from the very skirts,
Descend upon the open plain,
And bring each other to an end."
Is this not the true delight?
When we were in Talas,
Among all the Argyn and Kyrgyz,
This Choro who followed me
Resolved, "May I become a sacrifice
Before my elder brother;
May I pass on before him."
Such is exactly my resolve.
The ground of grappling is great turmoil;
The ground of clashing is great delight.
Do not grieve because I am young,
Blessed elder brother, leopard;
Do people not die while young?
Do not old and young alike meet
The decree laid down by the Creator?
My dear khan and elder brother,
Against Toltoy who has come to our border,
To give him his measured answer,
To die locked in combat,
I am the amulet hung upon the neck
Of the piebald herd's tulpar.
While still young, I long
To die once at Toltoy's hands.
If we shout and level spears
Against Toltoy of the Zhediger,
And fight him man to man,
If the spear strikes with a shriek,
If blood spills with a rush,
If Syrnayza, as we joust,
Splinters through the middle with a crack—
Would that not be splendid?
If you give me Akolpok, I shall wear it;
If you give me Arbuudan, I shall ride it.
I have my Buurul steed beneath me;
I have the strength to shatter
Not merely Toltoy, but Kaldang.
Listen to my words, mighty elder brother:
If I spear no man at twelve,
Will I, at thirty-five,
Catch even a tethered cow?"
Then your gray-maned lion, son of Manas,
As the boy stood pleading,
Saw God's sun cloud over in the sky,
And sixty worries came upon him:
"You mean to bring him face to face,
My dear Almighty,
With an inescapable sorrow;
What can I do, when you have made
A twelve-year-old boy gird his waist?
Külchoro, for a boy like you,
I would sacrifice my own dark life.
You are only a boy of twelve,
A soul whose time is still young.
If I grieve in sorrow,
What will our days become
If I lose you,
My companion, my Külchoro?
My ribs will be torn apart,
And tears will pour from my eyes;
Because you are your father's only son,
My heart is cruelly divided.
I have no mountain pass lying secure,
No place where I may gird my waist;
If hardship presses this toil-worn soul,
My renowned lion Bakay,
Who finds firm wisdom, is not here.
I came here among the Afghans;
None of the renowned Kyrgyz are here.
My elder Sarykhan, who would be
A binding support around my waist, is absent too.
There is no forest into which I can flee,
No stepmother on whom I can rely,
No cliff where even a goose cannot circle,
No rugged black mountain of mine.
I have no thoroughbred to ride out;
Sovereign God, it is only you,
And I have no kin except the boy.
"Semetey, Manas's boastful son—
He is as large as half a mountain.
"Meaning to take a wife from Afghanistan,
He had his two choros
Slaughtered together."
Do not go toward the jezail;
If God created you as a living soul,
Do not bring disgrace!
Do not reject my words.
I rely for companionship
Upon this lanky only boy;
O God, do not put me to shame.
Wearing his splendid motley coat,
The hero, son of Manas,
Paced along the road;
He slung around his neck
The Gray Purse left by Manas,
Preparing to give Külchoro
His battle dress.
When the gray-maned lion left Talas,
Your dear mother Kanykey
Had folded away upon a prayer rug
A form no person had yet seen,
Had it loaded upon Artelki:
A splendid white saddlebag.
Kanchoro flew swift as an arrow
And carried it in.
The white saddlebag bore no ornament;
Inside that saddlebag,
What was there, and what was not?
When they brought it and looked,
There was a helmet of blue iron,
Its inside lined with cotton and silk,
Its outside assembled from hardened steel,
Commissioned from Bölökbay,
Who had beaten smooth every flawed place;
Your mother who built the fortress
Had made every part fit perfectly:
"When the white banner comes,
When the shouting tumult comes,
The enemy will advance head-on,
And an axe may unexpectedly
Strike one of the boys."
Semetey paced with a rolling stride,
Showing that he was a hero;
He dressed Külchoro
In the charayna his mother had made.
He then took out another object;
Unless the Creator himself knew it,
Its workmanship was hard to comprehend.
Your dear mother Kanykey—
Could any woman be like this?
Could any woman prosper so?
Inside a single oak
She had hidden an object.
When they looked at that object,
Its collar was gold, its sleeves copper,
Double mail with lark-eye links.
Your heroic mother Kanykey
Had lined it inside with leather and silk,
Had iron assembled over its outside,
Had master after master test it,
Had its inner plates cast from hardened iron,
With double ribs of iron
And twin trailing straps, the remarkable thing,
Gathered together like slender rods.
